A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research despite the changed title. Their complete main texts, equations, eight figures, two tables, and appendices are readable and matchable, supporting a reliable comparison.

before.justification: V1 reports original experiments involving 112,710 responses from six LLMs, agent-transfer evaluations, mitigation comparisons, and supplementary analyses in the appendices.

after.justification: V2 retains those original experiments and additionally reports a 60-participant developer survey and human validation of 100 automatically labeled cases.

M1.justification: The emoticon collection, generate-and-fill pipeline, verification, weighted injection, and mitigation procedures are unchanged. V2's revised CR description clarifies functional-equivalence judging already documented in v1 Appendix A.2.2; it does not establish a changed algorithm.

E1.justification: V2 Appendix A.1 adds empirical coverage of experienced developers' self-reported emoticon use in everyday communication, general LLM interactions, and coding interactions. The original 3,757 test cases, 21 coding scenarios, four programming languages, and three contextual conditions remain unchanged.

E2.justification: Table 1 retains the same Base, Zero-shot CoT, ReAct, and System Instruction comparisons across the same six models. Self-refine remains mentioned in both appendices without a corresponding reported comparison row; no evaluated comparator is added or removed.

E3.justification: V2 introduces an online survey of 60 participants with at least one year of professional development experience and regular LLM coding use, plus human evaluation of 100 randomly sampled cases. Existing model evaluations, agent and mitigation subsets, and CR/CIR implementation remain unchanged.

E4.justification: V2 Appendix A.3.3 adds a human validation analysis testing the reliability of automated consequence labels. The existing scenario and context analyses, harm breakdowns, agent-transfer examples, case studies, and mitigation analyses are retained after appendix renumbering.

E5.justification: V2 newly reports chance-corrected agreement with human annotations using Cohen's kappa. The five queries per prompt, 1,000-sample bootstrap strategy, and stated significance-testing practice remain unchanged; no new confidence intervals are supplied.

E6.justification: V2 adds survey results: 43/60 participants use emoticons in daily communication, 16/60 in general LLM interactions, and 14/60 in coding interactions, with respective LLM daily-use counts of five and two. It also reports kappa 0.94 for the human validation. Existing benchmark, agent-transfer, mitigation, and appendix results remain unchanged.

T1.justification: The sample-tuple definition, emoticon substitution equation, contextual categories, CR/CIR formulas, and impact taxonomy are unchanged. Neither version contains formal theorems or proofs, and naming Cohen's kappa adds no mathematical derivation.

C1.justification: The core contributions and claims remain the identification of emoticon semantic confusion, the dataset-generation pipeline, widespread confusion and executable misinterpretations, agent transferability, and weak prompt-based mitigation. The survey and human validation provide additional support without redefining these claims.

C2.justification: V2 interprets the new survey as evidence of real-world coding relevance and the human validation as support for consequence-label reliability. These are limited additions; the existing mechanism explanations, failure scenarios, security implications, and dataset/model limitations remain unchanged.

D1.justification: The resource-access information changes from an anonymous 4open.science repository to the named GitHub project, including the reference for generation templates. Existing prompts, generation parameters, model-access details, hardware, and approximately $500 API cost remain unchanged. Repository availability is not independently verified.

R1.justification: V2 adds the xhs (2025) social-media incident citation to corroborate real-world harm. The scholarly related-work discussion and novelty positioning are otherwise unchanged; the renamed repository reference identifies the same project.

P1.justification: V2 changes the title and author-contact information, adds a corresponding-author designation, makes limited terminology edits, and rewrites the CR overview for clarity. A new survey subsection shifts appendix numbering, while the overall narrative and section organization remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: All eight figures and two tables are retained. Figure 2's caption is expanded, Figure 7 moves from PDF page 16 to page 15, and text reflow changes figure placement and removes substantial blank space around the conclusion and references. No substantive graphical redesign occurs.

improvement.justification: V2 adds useful checks absent from v1: the developer survey supports practical relevance, and the 100-case human validation provides evidence for automated-label reliability. Clarifying functional-equivalence judging also improves the main text's accuracy. These gains are limited by sparse survey and annotation-procedure details; the central experiments and conclusions remain unchanged.
